title: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis presenting as a neurological emergency: a case report
case_prompt:
A 65-year-old right-handed woman with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heavy smoking history, and bipolar disorder was transferred to the neurological intensive care unit after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Three weeks earlier, mediastinoscopic biopsy of a right hilar mass had confirmed small-cell lung cancer, but treatment had not yet begun. Shortly after biopsy, her family noted intermittent confusion that over two days progressed to fever, dizziness, vomiting, poor appetite, and progressive shortness of breath. She became increasingly lethargic and confused, failing to recognize family members. She was treated empirically for right lower lobe pneumonia with ceftriaxone and azithromycin without improvement in mental status.

At the local hospital, CSF analysis showed 28 white blood cells (99% lymphocytes), glucose 122 g/L, protein 36 g/L, no organisms on Gram stain, and no growth on bacterial culture. Brain MRI revealed bilateral mesial temporal hyperintensities on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences without contrast enhancement, diffusion restriction, or susceptibility changes. EEG demonstrated background slowing with focal sharp and slow discharges in the right mid-temporal and right posterior temporal regions. Intravenous acyclovir and fosphenytoin were started after she had a second generalized tonic-clonic seizure, and she was intubated and transferred.

On arrival, she was unresponsive to verbal or noxious stimuli, with intact brainstem reflexes but no purposeful movements. A second generalized tonic-clonic seizure with left gaze deviation occurred; EEG showed bilateral independent periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges in both temporal lobes, right-predominant. Lorazepam, phenytoin, levetiracetam, and topiramate were administered. Repeat CSF showed 23 white blood cells (94% lymphocytes) and was otherwise normal; cytology was negative for malignant cells. HSV PCR was negative on two occasions. Tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, varicella zoster virus, and human herpesvirus 6 were all negative. Repeat brain MRI confirmed bilateral mesial temporal T2-FLAIR hyperintensities without diffusion restriction or enhancement. Chest imaging showed post-obstructive pneumonia of the right lower lobe, collapse of the right middle and upper lobes, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and a loculated pleural effusion. Her lung cancer was deemed unresectable, and chemotherapy with carboplatin and etoposide was initiated once her pneumonia improved.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis — “Empiric treatment with acyclovir for HSV encephalitis continued until a second negative CSF HSV PCR returned.”  
2. Other viral encephalitides (EBV, CMV, VZV, HHV-6) — “Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), varicella zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) were all negative.”  
3. Brain metastases — “MRI of the brain showed T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in both mesial temporal regions without contrast enhancement…”  
4. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis — “CSF cytology did not show any malignant cells.”  
5. Post-obstructive pneumonia — “pneumonia might have contributed initially, but even after treatment of the pneumonia, the neurological status of our patient continued to decline.”
